articles.title: America's Doctors Are About to Learn About Food for the First Time. Here Is Why NRI Patients Should Care.
articles.excerpt: Seventy-three medical schools have pledged 40 hours of nutrition training. Licensing exams will test it. For South Asian patients whose food traditions were routinely dismissed, this is a watershed.
articles.image_caption: A nutritionist discusses healthy eating with a client surrounded by fresh produce
articles.nri_angle: South Asian patients have long faced physicians untrained in nutrition who dismissed food-based wellness traditions; this overhaul could finally bridge that gap.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Frozen Paratha May Be Wrecking Your Gut. A 124,000-Person Study Just Singled Out Ultraprocessed Grains.
articles.excerpt: The largest global study of its kind found that ultraprocessed grain intake nearly doubled the risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Fresh bread and rice were protective. The implications for diaspora kitchens are enormous.
articles.image_caption: Close-up of sliced whole grain bread on a wooden surface with wheat ears
articles.nri_angle: The shift from fresh roti and home-ground flour to frozen parathas, packaged naan, and instant noodles in NRI kitchens mirrors exactly the dietary transition this study links to gut disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Brain Starts Changing After Two Minutes of Meditation. Indian Scientists Just Proved It.
articles.excerpt: NIMHANS Bengaluru and Harvard tracked 103 meditators second-by-second and found the seven-minute sweet spot for breath-watching meditation.
articles.image_caption: A practitioner in focused breath-watching meditation
articles.nri_angle: An ancient Indian meditation practice studied at India's NIMHANS by Indian-origin Harvard researchers — validating what diaspora families practised for generations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The $275 Million Turmeric Myth: Why South Asian Kitchens Got It Right and the Supplement Industry Got It Wrong
articles.excerpt: Thirty papers retracted, curcumin barely detectable in the bloodstream, and turmeric supplements are now the top cause of herbal liver injury in the US. Here is what the diaspora needs to know.
articles.image_caption: Turmeric root and powder — safe in cooking, but concentrated supplements carry liver risks
articles.nri_angle: South Asian families have used turmeric in cooking for millennia — the supplement industry concentrated it into dangerous doses, while the kitchen had the right amount all along.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Scientists Just Mapped the 'Zombie Cells' Driving Ageing. The Implications for Your Parents Are Enormous.
articles.excerpt: A landmark NIH consortium has built the first comprehensive atlas of senescent cells across the human body, identifying blood biomarkers that predict kidney disease, frailty, and diabetes — and opening the door to drugs that could selectively destroy them.
articles.image_caption: Microscopy image of senescent cells — the 'zombie cells' that accumulate with ageing and drive chronic disease (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: With ageing parents back in India or living with family abroad, senolytic therapies could transform how the diaspora manages eldercare across borders.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: High Blood Pressure May Actually Protect Frail Elders From Dementia. A 6,000-Person Study Just Upended the Textbook.
articles.excerpt: A nine-year Neurology study found that elevated blood pressure cut dementia risk by 32 per cent in frail older adults — while raising it by 39 per cent in robust ones. For families managing ageing parents across borders, the implications are urgent.
articles.image_caption: Blood pressure measurement — a new study challenges conventional wisdom about hypertension management in frail elderly patients (Wikimedia Commons)

sources.label: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

articles.nri_angle: NRIs coordinating eldercare remotely need to understand that blood pressure targets for frail parents may differ sharply from standard guidelines — a conversation to have with doctors in India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Three Common Sleep Habits Are Silently Ageing Your Brain. A 23,000-Person Study Just Identified Them.
articles.excerpt: Sleeping too little, napping too often, and struggling to fall asleep were each independently linked to white matter damage — a marker of dementia risk.
articles.image_caption: An MRI brain scan showing white matter hyperintensities linked to cognitive decline
articles.nri_angle: South Asian communities face compounding sleep disruptors — intergenerational households, long-haul India travel, and cultural normalisation of napping — that make these findings especially urgent.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: South Asians Do Everything Right for Heart Health and Still Get Sick Earlier. A 2,700-Person Study Finally Explains Why.
articles.excerpt: Northwestern researchers found elevated rates of prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension in South Asian Americans by age 45 — despite healthier diets and lower alcohol use.
articles.image_caption: A blood pressure check — South Asian Americans show elevated cardiovascular risk factors by age 45 despite healthier habits
articles.nri_angle: South Asian Americans face a paradox: healthier habits yet higher cardiovascular risk by midlife, demanding earlier screening and South Asian-specific BMI thresholds.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Minutes of Exercise a Day Quadrupled Fitness in Adults Over 65. For the Diaspora, This Changes Everything About Aging Parents.
articles.excerpt: A Penn State study found that push-ups, chair stands, rows and stair steps — just 30 seconds each — produced dramatic strength gains in 12 weeks. The implications for NRI families managing elder care across oceans are profound.
articles.image_caption: A senior man performing push-ups at home as part of a daily fitness routine
articles.nri_angle: For millions of NRI families managing aging parents' health from thousands of miles away, a research-backed four-minute daily routine that requires no gym and no equipment beyond resistance bands could be the most practical intervention they can actually implement remotely.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Men and Women Need Different Diets to Live Longer. A 104,000-Person Study Just Proved It.
articles.excerpt: Coffee extends male lifespan by up to three years. Fish does the same for women. Both sexes benefit from cutting processed food — but the optimal longevity diet is not one-size-fits-all, and the South Asian kitchen may already hold the advantage.
articles.image_caption: Grilled fish with fresh vegetables and spices — the Mediterranean staples linked to female longevity
articles.nri_angle: The study's findings align strikingly well with traditional Indian dietary patterns — high legume and vegetable intake, extensive use of spices and turmeric, fish-heavy coastal cuisines, and daily coffee or tea rituals — suggesting that diaspora families preserving these food traditions may already be on the right track.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Daily Pill Just Doubled Pancreatic Cancer Survival. The Audience at ASCO Gave It a Standing Ovation.
articles.excerpt: Daraxonrasib is the first drug ever to meaningfully extend life in metastatic pancreatic cancer — a disease that kills 95 per cent of patients within five years. For South Asians, whose pancreatic cancer rates are climbing, the breakthrough could not be more urgent.
articles.image_caption: A researcher examines pharmaceutical compounds in a laboratory setting
articles.nri_angle: Pancreatic cancer incidence is rising among South Asians in India and abroad; daraxonrasib's oral delivery and universal mechanism offer hope regardless of geography or healthcare access.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ninety Minutes of Weights Per Week Cut Dementia Deaths by 27 Per Cent. South Asians Cannot Afford to Ignore This.
articles.excerpt: A 30-year Harvard study of 147,000 adults found that moderate resistance training slashed death from neurological disease, heart disease, and all causes — with a ceiling effect that makes the prescription achievable for anyone.
articles.image_caption: A man lifts heavy dumbbells during a strength training session at a gym
articles.nri_angle: South Asians have among the lowest exercise rates globally and face elevated cardiovascular and dementia risk; this study offers a specific, achievable prescription.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Single Brain Injection Restored Dopamine in 87% of Parkinson's Patients. The Gene Therapy Era May Have Arrived.
articles.excerpt: A Phase 1 trial of BBM-P002, a dual-target gene therapy, showed sustained motor improvement after 12 months with no serious side effects — offering hope to the estimated one million Indians living with Parkinson's and to diaspora families watching from abroad.
articles.image_caption: A digital rendering of the human brain, illustrating the neural pathways targeted by gene therapy
articles.nri_angle: Parkinson's disease affects an estimated one million Indians and is rising sharply in the diaspora; gene therapy breakthroughs will reach high-income countries first, leaving NRI families navigating a two-tier access system.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Heart Scan That Saved Millions of Lives Just Got Its First AI Upgrade. For South Asians, It Could Not Have Come Sooner.
articles.excerpt: Agatston-2.0, published in the American Journal of Preventive Cardiology, uses artificial intelligence to detect hidden coronary calcium in patients whose conventional scans showed a clean zero — a finding that matters disproportionately for a community with two to four times the average cardiovascular risk.
articles.image_caption: A CT scanner used for cardiac imaging in a modern hospital facility
articles.nri_angle: South Asians suffer heart attacks at younger ages and higher rates than almost any other ethnic group; an AI upgrade that catches early coronary calcium missed by conventional scans could save thousands of diaspora lives.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Joint Pain Pill Millions Take May Be Accelerating Alzheimer's. A 60,000-Patient Study Just Flagged It.
articles.excerpt: Glucosamine, one of the world's most popular over-the-counter supplements, is linked to a 25 per cent faster progression from mild cognitive impairment to dementia — and the mechanism may involve sugar molecules hijacking brain proteins.
articles.image_caption: Supplement capsules spilling from a white bottle
articles.nri_angle: Glucosamine is widely used among South Asian families for joint and knee pain, making this finding directly relevant to older NRIs and their parents back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Americans Born After 1970 Are Dying Faster Than Their Parents Did. The Data Is Alarming.
articles.excerpt: A Tufts University study tracking 45 years of mortality data reveals that Gen Xers and elder millennials face rising death rates from heart disease, cancer, and drug overdoses — reversing a century of progress that many immigrant families took for granted.
articles.image_caption: A doctor examines a middle-aged patient during a routine health check
articles.nri_angle: Many NRIs moved to America expecting better health outcomes for their families, but this data shows the country they adopted is quietly failing an entire generation — including their own children growing up here.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Gut Bacteria Could Fight Cancer: The Probiotic Trial That's Rewriting Oncology
articles.excerpt: A first-of-its-kind clinical trial is testing whether a common gut bacterium can supercharge cancer immunotherapy, with implications for South Asian patients who face some of the highest cancer rates globally
articles.image_caption: Microscopic view of gut bacteria, the trillions of microorganisms that may hold the key to better cancer treatment
articles.nri_angle: South Asian cancer rates, traditional fermented foods, NRI healthcare navigation
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Why You Walk Slower as You Age — and What Science Says You Can Do About It
articles.excerpt: A new study from Australia reveals the surprising neuromuscular reasons behind age-related gait decline, with urgent lessons for aging NRI parents and the diaspora communities caring for them
articles.image_caption: Pedestrians walking on a street in Hyderabad, India
articles.nri_angle: Aging NRI parents, fall prevention for elderly in India and abroad, diaspora caregiving challenges
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Harvard Study Links Ultraprocessed Foods to 58% Higher Dementia Risk — A Wake-Up Call for the Diaspora Diet
articles.excerpt: Researchers tracked 5,300 Americans for nearly a decade. Processed meats showed the strongest link to cognitive decline.
articles.image_caption: Ultraprocessed foods — from packaged snacks to reconstituted meats — have been linked to significantly higher dementia risk in a new Harvard study.
articles.nri_angle: South Asian immigrants transitioning from traditional whole-food diets to Western ultraprocessed diets face elevated dementia risk, especially as ready-made Indian snacks and frozen meals increasingly replace home-cooked food.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Low Vitamin C Levels Linked to Smaller, Less Connected Brains in New Study — And South Asian Diets May Offer an Edge
articles.excerpt: Japanese researchers scanned 2,000 brains and found that higher vitamin C in the blood correlated with more grey matter and stronger neural networks.
articles.image_caption: Higher vitamin C levels in the blood were associated with greater grey matter volume and stronger brain connectivity in adults over 64.
articles.nri_angle: Traditional South Asian diets are naturally rich in vitamin C through amla (Indian gooseberry), citrus fruits, guava, and fresh chutneys — a dietary advantage that may help protect brain health as the diaspora ages.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Eating Five Fruits and Vegetables a Day May Not Be Enough to Protect Your Heart, Major Study Finds
articles.excerpt: A new analysis of over 30,000 adults reveals that fewer than one in four people eating the recommended five daily servings of fruits and vegetables actually get enough flavanols to reduce cardiovascular risk — and the fix may already be in your chai cup
articles.image_caption: A heart-shaped bowl of fresh raspberries and blueberries — berries are among the richest dietary sources of flavanols linked to cardiovascular protection
articles.nri_angle: Many South Asian dietary staples — green tea, apples with skin, broad beans, and dark berries — are among the richest flavanol sources, putting Indian-origin households closer to the 500mg target than they might realise.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ninety-Seven of 104 World Cup Matches Face Significant Heat Risk: What Fans Travelling From India Need to Know
articles.excerpt: Climate scientists warn that the 2026 FIFA World Cup across the US, Mexico, and Canada could be the hottest major sporting event in history — and millions of South Asian fans heading to stadiums need a survival plan
articles.image_caption: Players compete under bright sunshine on a football pitch — climate scientists warn that 97 of 104 World Cup 2026 matches face significant heat risk
articles.nri_angle: Millions of South Asian fans in North America plan to attend World Cup matches this summer; extreme heat at open-air US stadiums poses a serious health risk that requires advance preparation.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Takeda's AI-Designed Psoriasis Pill Clears Skin 2.5 Times Better Than Rival — What It Means for South Asians
articles.excerpt: The once-daily oral drug zasocitinib outperformed the market leader in a landmark head-to-head trial, offering hope for an underdiagnosed community
articles.image_caption: Takeda Pharmaceutical's headquarters — the company's AI-designed psoriasis drug outperformed rivals in Phase 3 trials (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: South Asians face underdiagnosed psoriasis with high metabolic comorbidity; an effective oral pill could replace costly injectable biologics for NRI patients.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Breathing Dirty Air Could Be Silently Rewiring Your Brain for Alzheimer's, Major Study Finds
articles.excerpt: A landmark study in Molecular Psychiatry reveals that PM2.5 air pollution triggers DNA changes linked to pre-clinical Alzheimer's — and South Asians face disproportionate exposure.
articles.image_caption: Dense smog blankets Delhi, one of the world's most polluted cities, where PM2.5 levels routinely exceed WHO limits by 10-15 times.
articles.nri_angle: South Asians who grew up in India's polluted cities may carry invisible neurological risks — and those returning for extended visits face renewed exposure that this research suggests could accelerate Alzheimer's pathology.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Turmeric Pill Myth: Why Science Says Curcumin Supplements Aren't Doing What You Think
articles.excerpt: Despite billions spent on curcumin supplements worldwide, new research confirms what scientists have suspected — the compound barely reaches your bloodstream and has failed every rigorous clinical trial.
articles.image_caption: Turmeric roots (Curcuma longa) — the source of curcumin, a compound that shows promise in lab studies but consistently fails to deliver results in the human body.
articles.nri_angle: For South Asians who grew up with haldi doodh as medicine and now spend hundreds on curcumin capsules, the science is clear: the golden spice works best in your dal, not in a pill.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: 14 Indian Cities Now Rank Among the World's Most Heat-Vulnerable. The Plans to Save Them Are Falling Short
articles.excerpt: An Oxford study, new WHO guidance, and a Nature interview converge on the same conclusion: India needs systems-level heat resilience, not seasonal emergency responses
articles.image_caption: Indian cities are warming at 0.53°C per decade — an Oxford study placed 14 Indian urban centres among the world's 50 most heat-vulnerable

sources.label: University of Oxford / Sustainable Cities and Societies
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

articles.nri_angle: NRIs planning summer travel should note that 14 Indian cities are now among the world's 50 most heat-vulnerable. Diaspora professionals in climate tech and public health can contribute to the South Asia Heat Resilience Hub.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Weight-Loss Drug Has a Dangerous Summer Secret
articles.excerpt: GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Wegovy suppress thirst, increase fluid loss, and may impair water retention — turning this summer's heat waves into a medical minefield for one in eight American adults
articles.image_caption: GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Wegovy impair the body's thirst signals and temperature regulation — a hidden risk during extreme summer heat
articles.nri_angle: NRI travelers on GLP-1 medications face compounded risk during summer visits to India, where temperatures exceed 47°C. South Asian Americans also face higher GLP-1 adoption rates due to elevated diabetes and metabolic syndrome prevalence.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Two Diabetes Drugs Most Indians Take May Double the Risk of a Heart Attack. A 132,000-Patient Study Just Proved It.
articles.excerpt: Sulfonylureas and basal insulin are cheap and everywhere. A new JAMA study says they come at a hidden cardiovascular cost that South Asians can least afford.
articles.image_caption: A blood glucose test — a major new study links two widely prescribed diabetes drugs to doubled cardiovascular risk (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: South Asians have among the world's highest diabetes rates, and sulfonylureas remain the dominant treatment in India due to cost — this study shows that affordability may come at a deadly cardiovascular price for millions of NRI families managing care remotely.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Just Declared Children's Screen Time a Public Health Crisis. Some of the Damage May Be Permanent.
articles.excerpt: The Surgeon General set the strictest-ever federal limits on digital device use. A companion study says developmental windows missed to screens may never reopen.
articles.image_caption: A child playing with a smartphone in Kolkata, India
articles.nri_angle: South Asian families in the US are among the most device-connected households in the country, and cultural reliance on video calls with family in India complicates blanket screen restrictions — this advisory forces a calibration conversation that goes beyond simple time limits.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Medically Tailored Meals Cut Hospitalisations by 31 Per Cent. For the Diaspora, This Is More Than Vindication.
articles.excerpt: The largest Medicaid study on 'food is medicine' just proved what South Asian kitchens have practised for centuries. Now the healthcare system is catching up.
articles.image_caption: Medically tailored meals (Pexels)
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A New Obesity Drug Cuts Liver Fat by 63 Per Cent. For South Asians, That Changes the Conversation.
articles.excerpt: Survodutide attacks two conditions the diaspora carries disproportionately — obesity and fatty liver disease — in a single injection. But the side-effect profile demands scrutiny.
articles.image_caption: Medical illustration showing the stages of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease progression
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Three Common Sleep Habits Are Quietly Damaging Your Brain. A 23,000-Person Study Just Named Them.
articles.excerpt: Sleeping too little, napping too often, and chronic insomnia were all linked to white matter lesions that precede Alzheimer's. For South Asians, the risk profile hits close to home.
articles.image_caption: Brain MRI scan showing white matter hyperintensities, areas of damage linked to cognitive decline and dementia risk
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
